summary: The Users' Security Handbook is a companion to the Site Security Handbook. It gives ordinary users practical guidance for helping keep their networks and systems secure. It is informational advice rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a safety guide for everyday computer users, like a list of good habits for locking doors and not talking to strangers, but for computers.

subtitle: Plain advice for ordinary computer users on keeping their data, accounts and networks safe, written in 1999.

tldr.problem: Ordinary users, at work or at home, need practical guidance on protecting their accounts, privacy and systems, and administrators need something to build a site-specific guide from.
tldr.mechanism: The handbook gives rules of thumb in two parts, one for users on centrally administered networks and one for people who administer their own computers, plus a glossary of security terms.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational companion to the Site Security Handbook. Its own final note warns that examples may go out of date as the Internet and computer industry grow.

today: RFC 2504 is an Informational document (FYI 34), and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself cautions that its examples may become irrelevant as the Internet and computer industry grow.

sections.title: Who the Handbook Is For
sections.content:
The Users' Security Handbook is the companion to the Site Security Handbook (RFC 2196). It tells end-users what they can do to keep their data and communication private and their systems secure. Part Two addresses corporate users in small, medium and large corporate and campus sites. Part Three addresses people who administer their own computers, such as home users.

System and network administrators may use it as the foundation of a site-specific users' guide, but should consult the Site Security Handbook first. A glossary of security terms is included as an appendix. Before connecting, a user should obtain and read the site's security policy, the formal statement of rules that users must follow.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a rulebook for regular computer users, one chapter for people at a workplace and one for people at home.

sections.title: The Wires Have Ears
sections.content:
The handbook says it is a lot easier to eavesdrop on data networks than to tap a telephone conversation, and that all information passing over a network may be read by others. A user's first concerns should be protecting their accounts from misuse and then protecting their privacy.

Many network services ask for an account ID and password. If these are sent without encryption they can be intercepted. Programs such as telnet and ftp send user name, password and data unencrypted. Larger institutions commonly use one-time password systems against this, and the handbook names Secure Shell as a cryptographic technique that is available for many platforms and can also encrypt data on the wire.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything you send over a network can be overheard, like talking loudly in a crowded room. So secrets should be put in a locked box before they travel.

sections.title: Advice for Users on Managed Networks
sections.content:
Part Two gives these rules of thumb: know your security point-of-contact, keep passwords secret, use a password-locked screensaver or log out when you leave your desk, limit physical access to your computer, be wary of software of unknown origin, do not panic, and report problems quickly.

The details cover several topics. Downloading is called the single greatest risk, and any file loaded over the network, even one in a browser cache, should be treated as possibly dangerous. Web forms are not secure unless something like SSL is used, and a page can be a forgery, so users can check a page's certificate. Email can be forged, is potentially visible along its path, and attachments are files like any other. Employers may in some cases legally read work email.

For passwords, the handbook recommends a mixture of numbers, letters and punctuation, no real words, never writing them where others can see, never saving them in scripts, different passwords for different accounts and periodic changes. It also advises permission before attaching equipment, care with modems (turn auto-answer off unless needed), setting file permissions, encrypting private files, and shredding documents before discarding them. Deleting a file does not erase it in many cases.
sections.plainLanguage: At work you should keep your password secret, lock your screen when you walk away, and be careful with anything you download or open, because it might be a trick.

sections.title: Social Engineering
sections.content:
Section 4 argues that many break-ins are not purely technical. Social engineering is gaining the trust of legitimate users until they reveal secrets or unintentionally help an attacker. The handbook says most attackers using it work by telephone, which hides their identity.

Its examples include pretending to be a new or confused user who needs help, posing as a VIP to pressure administrators, offering help to a frustrated user, and getting users to type commands they do not understand. The defense is simple: a personal password should be known only to its owner, administrators do not need it, accounts should not be shared, and visiting technicians should be accompanied by a site administrator the user knows. If you cannot verify who you are talking to, reveal no secrets.
sections.plainLanguage: Some bad guys do not break the lock, they just ask nicely and pretend to be someone you trust. Never give out your secret word, even to someone who sounds important.

sections.title: Advice for Home and Self-Administered Users
sections.content:
Part Three tells users who run their own machines to decide ahead of time what risks are acceptable, review that decision regularly, turn on security features, and prepare for the worst. Preparation includes backing up data, installing virus checking or auditing tools before connecting, upgrading networking software regularly, and knowing who to contact at the Internet service provider.

The handbook lists three ways to avoid viruses: be cautious about what software is installed, scan regularly, and notice the unusual. A detection tool should be up to date, not older than three months. If a system may be compromised, disconnect it from all networks; ideally rebuild from original distribution media rather than backups, since the backups may already contain altered files.

Home systems that run services such as file servers, FTP servers or web servers, called daemons, face the greatest risk if misconfigured or unpatched. Users should enable security logging, review the logs, and secure remote logins with technologies like one-time passwords, SSH and SSL.
sections.plainLanguage: At home you are your own security guard. Keep a spare copy of your files, keep your protection programs fresh, and if something goes wrong, unplug from the network first.

sections.title: Closing Note and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: the document discusses what computer users can do to improve security on their systems. The final note adds that security issues go out of date quickly, and that examples given may not be relevant in the future as the Internet and computer industry continue to grow.

It closes by comparing computer security to the extra care home-owners now take at the expense of convenience, concluding that it is always better to be safe than sorry.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say the exact tricks will change, but being careful is always a good idea, even when it is a little bit annoying.

viz.caption: THREE WAYS TO AVOID VIRUSES (RFC 2504, SECTION 6.1)

items.title: Do not be promiscuous
items.text: Be cautious about software you install and obtain it from trusted sources.

items.title: Scan regularly
items.text: Use virus checking and audit tools, set them to run automatically, and keep them updated.

items.title: Notice the unusual
items.text: Missing files, strange new files or vanishing disk space are reasons to check for viruses.
